source: Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) The evolution of foresight: What is mental time travel, and is it unique to humans? BBS 30:299-351
finding: Founding taxonomy. Memory systems differ in how flexibly they serve the future. Non-declarative systems give procedural prospection (stimulus-bound). Semantic memory gives semantic prospection. Episodic memory gives mental time travel (MTT), the most flexible and most recent system. They find no convincing evidence of MTT in animals.
numbers: Review with open peer commentary; no single N. Concludes 'no convincing evidence' for MTT in nonhuman animals as of 2007.
quote: MTT ... allows us not only to go back in time, but also to foresee, plan, and shape virtually any specific future event.
limits: The taxonomy is a conceptual claim, not a measured one. Authors admit absence of proof is not proof of absence. Commentators (e.g. Raby et al.) reject the claim that semantic prospection is inferior.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean ladder for prospection in an agent: reactive prediction, retrieval of general knowledge, then flexible scene construction decoupled from current input. Useful vocabulary for what a scaffold lacks or has.

source: Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) BBS: Bischof-Kohler hypothesis and theater metaphor
finding: Bischof-Kohler hypothesis (BKH): animals cannot act now for a future need state that differs from the current drive. Suddendorf and Busby proposed a nonverbal test: control the current need (e.g. not thirsty), then offer a chance to secure a future need. The hypothesis becomes untenable if one animal passes variants across needs (hunger, thirst, temperature) and contexts. The 'theater metaphor' lists component skills: stage (secondary representation), director (executive control, inhibition), recursion, prospective memory, imagining own future mental states.
numbers: Passing across several needs and contexts is the stated falsification bar. Children are said to anticipate future needs by about age 4 (Suddendorf and Busby 2005); unequivocal episodic memory emerges around ages 3-5.
quote: nonverbal tests of the Bischof-Kohler hypothesis ... involve controlling a current need state
limits: Predictions were stated before Raby 2007 and later tests. Authors argue for non-species-typical behaviour (not caching) to rule out innate predispositions.
agent_relevance: The BKH test design (decouple current state from future state) is a direct template for testing whether an LLM agent plans for a need it does not currently have in context. Component list maps to scaffold parts: executive inhibition, prospective memory, self-state prediction.

source: Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) BBS: critique of Mulcahy and Call 2006 and Raby 2007
finding: Mulcahy and Call: apes chose a suitable tool on average 7 of 16 trials, best orangutan 15 of 16; overnight delay still above chance. S&C reply: same tools were right on every trial, so apes could have learned a fixed rule; the control group was a new set of 4 animals, and 2 of them never brought a tool back so could not have been rewarded. Raby et al: 8 jays; counterbalancing meant 4 expected no breakfast and 4 expected breakfast, but results were pooled; a general 'balance food sources' heuristic is an alternative.
numbers: Mulcahy and Call 7/16 trials correct on average (single orangutan 15/16). Raby: N=8 jays, 6 training mornings, one test evening.
limits: This is the authors' reading, not the original data. Raby et al responded in the same issue that S&C did not give testable criteria.
agent_relevance: Shows the standard objection pattern: a pass is dismissed by a simpler rule (learned heuristic). Any claim that an agent 'plans' needs a control that separates planning from a learned rule.

source: Raby, Alexis, Dickinson, Clayton (2007) Planning for the future by western scrub-jays. Nature 445:919-921
finding: Founding caching-planning study. Jays learned they would be hungry the next morning in one compartment and fed in another, then cached more food where they would be hungry (Exp 1: planning for breakfast). In Exp 2 they cached each food type in the place where that food would not be available next morning. Authors say this is spontaneous planning without reference to current motivation.
numbers: Abstract page read. Per S&C's account: 8 jays, six mornings of training, a single caching test evening. Exact cache counts were not available to me (full text paywalled).
quote: jays can spontaneously plan for tomorrow without reference to their current motivational state
limits: Abstract and figure captions only; full text not opened. Later work failed to replicate in Eurasian jays (Amodio 2021) and in Canada jays (Martin 2021).
agent_relevance: A single-test, no-retrieval design is the key strength: no feedback from earlier outcomes. For an agent, the analog is acting on a one-shot expectation with no reinforcement history.

source: Correia, Dickinson, Clayton (2007) Western scrub-jays anticipate future needs independently of their current motivational state. Curr Biol 17:856-861
finding: Used specific satiety to separate current from future desire. Jays fed one food cached the other, then were fed so that at recovery they wanted a different food; after a few trials they cached the food they would want at recovery, not the one they wanted at caching. Challenges the BKH.
numbers: Per Paxton and Hampton 2009 and Cheke and Clayton 2012: 3 h caching-to-recovery delay; by trial 3 the 'same' group kept caching the non-pre-fed food, the 'different' group shifted to the pre-fed food. Exact N not read.
limits: Abstract read directly; numbers from secondary sources. Critique (Suddendorf and Corballis 2008): the different group only reduced caching of the sated food, did not increase the pre-fed food, so 'learning what not to cache' is possible. Needed learning across trials (not spontaneous).
agent_relevance: Shows planning may be built by fast learning plus anticipation of a state change. Relevant for agents: the 'future self wants X' model must be tested against learned avoidance.

source: Cheke and Clayton (2012) Eurasian jays overcome their current desires to anticipate two distinct future needs and plan for them appropriately. Biol Lett 8:171-175
finding: Within-subject version with a new species. Jays cached in two trays; one tray would be opened after the same pre-feeding as at caching, the other after the other pre-feeding. They came to cache in each tray the food they would desire at retrieval from that tray. Answers the one-sided critique.
numbers: N=4 Eurasian jays. Specific satiety check: pre-fed food eaten/cached less (overall F(1,3)=12.4, p=0.039; caching F(1,3)=10.45, p=0.048). Planning: trial x tray x food interaction F(2,2)=24.95, p=0.039. Trial 1 baseline interaction F(1,3)=3.0, p=0.18; trial 2 F(1,3)=14.24, p=0.030; trial 3 F(1,3)=2.26, p=0.23. Caching differed from eating pattern F(1,3)=19.99, p=0.021. Three of 4 birds showed the pattern; one bird (Hunter) lost it in trial 3.
limits: Tiny N (4); the key interaction p=0.039 with 2 error df; effect lost in trial 3 (p=0.23). Authors suggest associative learning and future cognition may combine. Not replicated by the same lab in a later design (Amodio 2021 used a different protocol).
agent_relevance: Even the best-case positive result is N=4 with borderline statistics. Treat as a hint, not a measured capability; require larger N before building on 'planning for a future desire'.

source: Amodio, Brea, Farrar, Ostojic, Clayton (2021) Testing two competing hypotheses for Eurasian jays' caching for the future. Sci Rep 11:835
finding: Pre-registered attempt to separate the Future Planning Hypothesis (FPH) from the Compensatory Caching Hypothesis (CCH) in Eurasian jays, using a Raby-style design with three compartments. In both experiments neither hypothesis won. The best model was a uniform pattern with no compartment effect.
numbers: Exp 1: 6 birds tested; posterior probability 0.997 for 'bird and food type but not compartment' model; best FPH 0.0014; best CCH 0.00001. Without one bird (Lisbon) the FPH falls to 0.00008 and CCH rises to 0.0002. Exp 2 (pre-registered, OSF 3y5tm): 6 birds tested of 7; again compartment-independent model best. 13 models in Bayesian comparison.
limits: Small N (6). Design differed from Raby: food-location link changed on a 3-day/2-day cycle, birds group-housed, possible high cognitive load; authors say replication of both Raby and this study is needed.
agent_relevance: A rare failed replication using explicit Bayesian model comparison. The method (formalise rival hypotheses as likelihood models, then compare) is directly reusable for testing agent planning claims.

source: Amodio et al. (2021) formalisation of three hypotheses for caching for the future
finding: Three competing accounts of the jay results. (1) Future Planning: recall what-where-when of past events and predict future availability. (2) Mnemonic Association: long-delay learning at cache recovery strengthens the rewarded cache action. (3) Compensatory Caching: a standing tendency to cache a food where it was not recently found, which spreads resources and defends against theft. Mnemonic Association cannot explain Raby 2007 (single caching event); Compensatory Caching can.
numbers: Raby Exp 1: six consecutive days in A or C with food only for first two hours, then one caching opportunity on day 6. Field note cited: wild American crows carried walnuts up to 2 km before caching.
limits: Each alternative explains only a subset of studies; together they explain all published results (authors' claim).
agent_relevance: Teaches how to design controls: pick a test that makes rival hypotheses predict different outputs. An agent's 'planning' claim should survive a test where the 'habit' and 'plan' predictions diverge.

source: Martin, Martin, Roberts, Sherry (2021) No evidence for future planning in Canada jays. Biol Lett 17:20210504
finding: Close replication of Raby 2007 Preparing-for-Breakfast in 6 Canada jays, repeated three times. Birds cached more in the compartment where food was usually available (feeding) than where it was absent (fasting), the opposite of scrub-jays. Breakfast Choice could not be analysed because 3 birds made zero caches.
numbers: N=6. Feeding vs fasting compartment: F(1,15)=12.18, p<0.001 in the direction opposite to Raby. No compartment x iteration interaction F(1,15)=3.23, p=0.09. Mean caches per bird per iteration 8, 7.5, 8.5. One trial excluded (no caches).
limits: Species, wild-caught birds in captivity 8-18 months, light cycle shifted 1 h, different foods. Authors note scrub-jays may have had extensive captive caching experience. Not a direct test of the same species.
agent_relevance: Opposite-direction result shows the effect is not a general corvid trait. Warns that agent results found with one model or setup may flip with another; test across models.

source: Paxton and Hampton (2009) Tests of planning and the Bischof-Kohler hypothesis in rhesus monkeys. Behav Processes 80:238-246
finding: Rhesus monkeys did not give up a large food amount to avoid a longer wait for water later. Monkeys chose the large amount although it caused more thirst. Covering the food with opaque cups did not change this. This contrasts with squirrel monkeys (Naqshbandi and Roberts 2006).
numbers: N=6 monkeys. Long (120 min) vs short (15 min) water delay: water drunk after delay 51.17 mL vs 40.83 mL, t(5)=-4.04, p=0.01. Large-amount choice above chance on baseline (t(5)=4.41 first block, 9.26 last) and stayed so in experimental trials. Exp 2 (opaque cups): last block t(5)=6.53, p<0.01 for the cup with large food and long delay.
limits: Only Exp 1 and 2 read in detail; later experiments in the paper not summarised here. Possible inhibition problem or species difference.
agent_relevance: Species-level negative results for BKH-style tasks. Shows the same task can fail through lack of inhibition rather than lack of prospection; an agent test must separate these.

source: Naqshbandi and Roberts (2006) Anticipation of future events in squirrel monkeys and rats: tests of the Bischof-Kohler hypothesis. J Comp Psychol 120:345-357
finding: Non-thirsty animals chose a smaller or larger food quantity; the large quantity induced thirst, and choosing the small quantity returned water sooner. Squirrel monkeys reversed their baseline preference for the larger amount; rats did not.
numbers: Abstract only; numbers not read. Species: squirrel monkeys (Saimiri sciureus), rats (Rattus norvegicus).
limits: Abstract only. Suddendorf and Corballis note monkeys may have acted from current motivation for the reward. Rhesus failed (Paxton and Hampton 2009).
agent_relevance: A delay-for-need task is easy to adapt as an agent probe (reward trade vs later resource shortfall).

source: Mulcahy and Call (2006) Apes save tools for future use. Science 312:1038-1040
finding: Bonobos and orangutans selected, carried and saved suitable tools above baseline to use them 1 hour later (Exp 1); effect held at a 14-hour delay (Exp 2) and when the apparatus was not visible during selection (Exp 3).
numbers: Per S&C 2007: 2 suitable and 6 unsuitable tools; average 7/16 trials correct, best orangutan 15/16.
limits: Abstract read; numbers from S&C. Tools were the same on every trial; need was for the tool to satisfy current desire for grapes (S&C 2007, Suddendorf et al. 2009).
agent_relevance: The 'spoon test' paradigm: choose now, use later in a different place. Good agent analogy: choose a tool or note now for a task that appears later.

source: Kabadayi and Osvath (2017) Ravens parallel great apes in flexible planning for tool-use and bartering. Science 357:202-204
finding: Ravens planned for tool use and bartering (not caching) with delays up to 17 hours, exerted self-control, and weighed temporal distance. Shows planning beyond the caching adaptation.
numbers: Abstract only: delay up to 17 hours. N not read.
limits: Abstract only. Associative explanations were contested later (see Boeckle 2020 design rationale).
agent_relevance: Evidence that planning generalises across domains, the criterion S&C set for BKH.

source: Osvath and Osvath (2008) Chimpanzee and orangutan forethought: self-control and pre-experience in the face of future tool use. Anim Cogn 11:661-674
finding: Four experiments: chimpanzees and orangutans overrode immediate drives for future needs (tool use) and did not rely only on associative learning or semantic prospection. Authors link to self-control and mental pre-experience.
numbers: Abstract only; four experiments, N not read.
limits: Abstract only. Suddendorf et al. 2009 argue controls were inadequate.
agent_relevance: Highlights self-control (suppress immediate reward) as a separate component the agent could implement as a budget gate.

source: Boeckle, Schiestl, Frohnwieser, Gruber, Miller, Suddendorf, Gray, Taylor, Clayton (2020) New Caledonian crows plan for specific future tool use. Proc R Soc B 287:20201490
finding: Pre-registered spoon test designed by researchers on both sides of the debate. Crows saw a baited apparatus, 5 min later chose among 5 objects, 10 min later got the apparatus. Distractors had been tools for another apparatus and a low-value food item was present. Three of four crows chose the right tool for the future task in novel combinations.
numbers: 9 crows entered; 6 reached training, 4 reached criterion in 20-25 trials. Test conditions 3 and 4: Neptune 9/10, Uranus 7/10, Triton 7/10 correct, Saturn 3/10 (p=0.429); binomial against 5 choices p<0.001 for the three. Training learning effect only when the 4 pass-criterion crows are analysed (trial z=2.155, p=0.031).
limits: Small N; only 4 of 9 passed the training criterion; all successful crows female; associative learning not fully ruled out; trained tool use not natural behaviour. Reanalysis with 3 options still significant.
agent_relevance: Best-designed positive result. Its design (distractors valuable elsewhere, temporal gaps, novel combos) is a good template for an agent probe.

source: Esteve and Santariello (2021) New test, old problems: comment on Boeckle et al. Proc R Soc B 288
finding: Argues Boeckle's design still allows a first-order explanation: crows can act correctly whether or not they represent a future. Associative learning and 'higher-order representation' are not truly alternative hypotheses.
numbers: No data; a table splits each step into first-order and higher-order representations. Passing time without sight of the apparatus has not been shown to remove prior training effects.
limits: Commentary; philosophical argument. A reply by Boeckle's group exists (not opened).
agent_relevance: The same regress will apply to LLM planning claims: any pass can be redescribed as pattern learning. Need behavioural dissociations, not labels.

source: Clayton and Dickinson (1998) Episodic-like memory during cache recovery by scrub jays. Nature 395:272-274
finding: Founding what-where-when paradigm. Jays cached perishable wax worms and nonperishable peanuts, then recovered after short or long delay. They searched for worms after a short delay and for peanuts after a long delay, once they had learned worms decay.
numbers: Per 2025 revisit: 4 h vs 124 h delays; first caching trial then 120 h wait, second caching, then recovery. Only birds that had experienced decayed worms showed the pattern. Original N not read.
limits: Abstract read directly; design details from Davies and Clayton 2025 revisit. Criticisms: associative or familiarity explanations. Later controls ruled out some (Clayton and Dickinson 1999a-c).
agent_relevance: Source of the episodic-like memory idea; supports the principle that future-oriented behaviour reuses what-where-when records. For agents: log events with what, where, when fields.

source: Davies, Clayton et al. (2025) Revisiting episodic-like memory in scrub jays. Learn Behav
finding: Previously unpublished replication and extension of C&D 1998 with finer behavioural measures. Searches went to the worm tray after a short delay and the pine-nut tray after a long delay numerically, but the key tests were weak. Authors call it a replication in spirit.
numbers: 4 birds completed both delays (8 in long delay only). First search short delay: all 4 went to the worm tray (p<0.001). Long delay: 1/4 first went to pine-nut tray (p=1; 3 of 8 in the 8-bird analysis, p=0.422). Cached-in vs control trays W=4, p=0.068; first 3 min chi2(1)=4, p=0.046; RMANOVA tray x delay F(1,3)=1.80, p=0.272.
limits: Very small samples; main interaction not significant; the lab's own account of 'replicates' is generous. Unpublished until 2025.
agent_relevance: Shows the 'classic result' is statistically fragile at small N. Record N and p when citing animal evidence for design choices.

source: Davies and Clayton (2024) Is episodic-like memory like episodic memory? Phil Trans R Soc B 379:20230397
finding: Review of what-where-when, incidental encoding with unexpected question, and source-memory paradigms. States the evidence is mixed. On planning: scrub-jays but not Canada jays plan for hunger; Eurasian and scrub jays defeat the BKH; rats and rhesus fail while squirrel monkeys pass; the Eurasian jay finding has failed to replicate; NC crows passed a pre-registered spoon test; cuttlefish show flexible future-dependent foraging.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Raby 2007, Correia 2007, Cheke and Clayton 2012, Martin 2021, Amodio 2021, Boeckle 2020, Billard 2020.
limits: Authors are from the lab that produced much of the positive evidence.
agent_relevance: Good current summary of the field's honest state: positive results in a few species, many conditional.

source: Huet, Ben Houidi, Rossi (2025) Episodic Memories Generation and Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models (ICLR 2025)
finding: Synthetic episodic-memory benchmark for LLMs with events grounded in time, space, entities. Cue overload hurts: F1 drops once a cue matches 2 or more events. Models also confabulate when no event matches.
numbers: Long book, in-context: no-match questions (n=150) F1 gpt-4o 0.84, claude-3.5-sonnet 0.92, o1-mini 0.97, gpt-4o-mini 0.51; single-match (n=150) gpt-4o 0.81, claude-3.5-sonnet 0.35, o1-mini 0.05; 6+ matches (n=60) gpt-4o 0.53. RAG 6+ matches 0.59-0.62. Fine-tuned gpt-4o-mini: 0.00 on no-match, 0.83 single match, 0.19 on 6+ matches.
limits: Tests recall of past events, not future simulation. Claude 3.5 Sonnet in-context affected by a verbosity bug (authors note). The paper only frames mental time travel in the introduction.
agent_relevance: Past-event retrieval underlies planning, and it degrades under cue overload and confabulates for absent events. A scaffold should store events with typed cues (time, place, entity) and handle the empty-match case explicitly.

source: Pink et al. (2025) Position: Episodic Memory is the Missing Piece for Long-Term LLM Agents. arXiv:2502.06975
finding: Position paper: LLM agents need episodic memory with five properties (single-shot learning of instance-specific contexts, etc.) and a roadmap uniting current research. No experiment.
numbers: No measurements (abstract page only).
limits: Abstract read only; no results. Not a test of prospection.
agent_relevance: Treat as design framing. Links episodic storage to future planning but supplies no evidence.

source: Towards large language models with human-like episodic memory. Trends Cogn Sci (2025)
finding: Review: popular memory-augmented LLM approaches are misaligned with human episodic memory in several ways; proposes benchmark criteria and neuroimaging comparisons.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; no data about future thinking.
agent_relevance: Suggests the field has no direct LLM test of mental time travel yet; open niche.

source: Search for LLM-specific tests of mental time travel, spoon test or BKH (2020-2026)
finding: I found no paper that runs a spoon test, a Bischof-Kohler test, or a caching-planning replication on an LLM. The nearest are episodic-memory benchmarks (Huet 2025) and position papers (Pink 2025). Searches used: one WebSearch (standard); the arXiv API returned nothing.
numbers: Zero direct LLM studies found; 2 adjacent works. Search was limited (1 web search, arXiv API empty); absence is not proven.
limits: Search coverage is partial because of shared-budget limits (OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar rate-limited).
agent_relevance: The gap is a chance: a BKH-style probe (act now for a state different from the present one) could be our own measurement.

source: Suddendorf and Corballis (2007) BBS: Raby et al. commentary and Schacter-Addis constructive episodic simulation
finding: Raby, Alexis, Dickinson, Clayton argue MTT is not testable as episodic vs semantic: the only difference may be the sensation of pre-experiencing, and the BKH is the tractable criterion. Schacter and Addis add the constructive episodic simulation hypothesis: future thinking needs flexible recombination of details from past events. The issue notes Shettleworth called Raby 2007 the first unambiguous animal future planning.
numbers: No numbers; text-level claims. Neuroimaging and amnesia work cited (Addis 2007, Hassabis 2007, Szpunar 2007).
limits: Commentary round in 2007, before the failed replications.
agent_relevance: Constructive simulation is the main computational idea: a plan is a recombination of stored event details. Fits a scaffold that rebuilds futures from stored episodes rather than from a single summary.

source: Suddendorf, Corballis, Collier-Baker (2009) How great is great ape foresight? Anim Cogn 12:751-754
finding: Cited in Davies and Clayton 2024 and S&C 2007 as the argument that ape tool-saving studies lack controls against associative explanation.
numbers: Not opened; known only through citation.
limits: Second-hand; unverified.
agent_relevance: Lists the control types an agent probe should include.
